This paper reviews key methodologies used to evaluate such data and introduces new visualizations designed for assessing data compositionality. These include various linear algebra-based approaches, for example, computing spectral decomposition via eigenvalue analysis of a specific covariance matrix, alongside proposed compositional plots that enhance diagnostic capabilities. The proposed methods are demonstrated through application to a well-known ecological dataset, illustrating both practical implications and interpretative insights.

Discovered by radial velocity methods, over 70% of known exoplanits exceed the 200 Earth-mass threshold. However, theorist predictions suggest that planets situated between super-Earth and sub-Saturn masses (roughly 10–20 $M_\oplus$ to < 1/30 $M_\text{Sat}$) should be more common than their super-Earth counterparts. This study utilizes a compiled dataset of minimum masses ($M \sin i$) exceeding 5 $M_\text{E}$ to test this hypothesis. Our findings indicate a pronounced scarcity of planets with masses just at or slightly above 2 $M_\text{E}$, contrary to expectations. Instead, the vast majority of systems host planets with minimum masses greater than 8 $M_\text{E}$. While current data fail to confirm an actual population gap, they reveal a strong bias away from low masses. This observed trend may stem from significant measurement uncertainties or a detection gap near the super-Earth boundary combined with a true desert at very low masses (specifically 5 $M_\text{E}$ to 8 $M_\text{E}$). If such a gap truly exists, it would likely be a consequence of the high surface gravity on massive cores capable of efficiently clearing nearby debris, thereby suppressing the formation of smaller neighbors.

Our study introduces a new method for monitoring and enhancing visual attention as an essential step toward building fully autonomous machine vision systems. This approach utilizes a fully convolutive neural network to generate an attention map from an input image, with its core mechanism being an objective function based on mutual information to ensure the map remains normalized against various images and transformations. To further enhance accuracy, we achieve an objective function for map refinement through end-to-end training alongside image registration and an optimal loss derivation for this purpose by using the defined mutual information as an anchor. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to comparable techniques while being significantly more straightforward to implement.

We investigate the interaction of dark matter (DM) with ordinary matter, assuming a contact interaction mediated by a light scalar or pseudoscalar particle. This setup allows DM particles to form bound states resembling hydrogen atoms, which we term "nuclei," while interactions with electrons generate repulsive or attractive Yukawa potentials between these particles. While prior research examined DM-nuclei annihilation via contact interactions yielding a $1/\rho$ potential profile, we extend this analysis by accountinging for both scalar and pseudoscalar mediators, which produce $r^{-2}$ and $r^{-1}$ terms (respectively) in the potential, with the attractive $r^{-1}$ component promoting system collapse. Focusing on the collapse scenario, we analyze DM-nuclei energy level structures and determine that the ground state of such a nucleus possesses binding energy substantially exceeding that of standard dark nuclei. In the regime of scalar mediators, we find that the annihilation cross section of these compressed systems is enhanced by orders of magnitude relative to conventional Nuclei, significantly influencing direct detection constraints. Regarding scalar systems, this enhancement renders DM in a highly compressed state essentially inaccessible to direct detection. Conversely, configurations mediated by pseudoscalars reduce DM mass in the compressed state proportionally to roughly a tenth of the original DM mass.

Radio-loud Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are hypothesized to regulate Cyclic feedback within early Universe galaxies and their surrounding regions. Observations of AGN populations at high redshifts are increasingly being gathered, though it remains uncertain whether the cosmic microwave background (CMB) plays a role in their evolution. This study examines CMB-driven linear and non-linear jet instabilities, as well as Nuclei-Induced Resonance Instabilities (NRI), to evaluate how the CMB might have shaped early-stage AGNs. Our findings suggest that the CMB influenced the development of these objects; specifically, the CMB could truncate the jet injection, potentially shaping conical structures, while NRI might redirect energy into perpendicular directions, thereby altering the energy distribution of radio-loud AGNs.

This analysis examines various forms of Lagrangian gravity and demonstrates that generic expressions lead to field equations lacking kinetic terms. As anticipated, solutions to these equations degenerate into constant configurations. We additionally propose a framework where the kinetic-free nature of the field equations emerges dynamically from the structure of the kinetic terms themselves.

This paper introduces a new approach for 3D medical image registration that leverages two key innovations: the integration of 3D SIFT for feature extraction and matching, and a voxel selection technique based on discrete rotational symmetry. While traditional methods often rely on manual landmarking or intensity-based optimization with limited initial ranges, our method automates this process by identifying landmarks within highly symmetric voxels. We define our selected features as those with rotational symmetry planes or points, initially using a discrete approximation of rotational invariant moments to screen candidates. To further refine candidate selection, we trained a binary classifier on data derived from the MICCAI 2012 Prostate 12 dataset to confirm landmark placement. Evaluations on the same dataset, conducted via both pairwise and batch protocols, demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms standard 3D registration using all voxels. Additionally, the framework was extended to support multiple image registrations. Testing on the MICCAI 2012 Prostate 12 set confirmed the method's high accuracy and efficiency.

Global pooling layers are essential components in deep learning architectures designed to aggregate feature maps by compressing spatial information into global feature descriptors. Although widely used, these layers often struggle with an excessive reliance on spatial locations, leading to retained incorrect locations in the final descriptors and poor generalization. To address this, we introduce a novel perspective based on viewing global pooling as an Ideal Transport problem, aiming to enhance global pooling layers and derived semantic segmentation models for improved performance and robustness. Specifically, this research proposes three primary contributions: (1) formulating global pooling as an Optimal Transport (OT) equation for a more precise theoretical analysis; (2) deriving an efficient global pooling layer by employing an Approximate Solution (AS) of the OT formulation; and (3) designing a parametrically learnable global pooling layer utilizing an Explicit Kernel OT (KOT) approach. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm that integrating the OT-based global pooling layer into deep neural networks yields significant improvements in both performance and robustness for semantic segmentation.

**Objectives.** We aim to investigate host galaxy characteristics and their structural alignment across different Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) classifications. **Appro.** We selected 1,000 Type 1 Seyferts, 1,000 Type 2 Seyfirts, and 1,000 Radio Galaxies, ensuring each class had an $r$-band absolute magnitude ($M_r$) ranging from -24 to -21. Using the $r$-$z$ color index, we classified these galaxies into Red, Blue, or Intermediate groups. **Results.** Our analysis reveals that Type 1 hosts are predominantly Blue, whereas both Type 2 and Radio Galaxies are mostly Red. Among the three AGN types, only Radio Galaxy hosts display a strong preference for major mergers. Furthermore, the angular distribution of polarizers in Radio Galaxy hosts is largely random, contrasting with the preference for perpendicular orientation found in other AGN classes. These observations suggest that AGN structural anisotropies are more pronounced in Radio Galaxies than in Seyfert galaxies.

Pre-training has emerged as a critical strategy for enhancing model performance in self-supervised semantic segmentation. This study investigates utilizing depth estimation as pre-training supervision. Experiments demonstrate that such depths can surpass other common categorization-based pre-training methods. To achieve these results, we introduce a new pre-training framework guided by noisy depth estimation. Our findings indicate that deeper models benefit significantly from this approach; specifically, it works best with very deep architectures where intermediate layers are also pre-trained. To further boost efficiency, we propose conditioning depth estimation on the outputs of these hidden layers, rather than applying it solely at the final layer. Additionally, we address the high computational cost of this training step by proposing a caching strategy that accelerates execution by up to 4×. Our experiments show that pre-training with this imperfect depth data yields superior representations for segmentation tasks compared to using perfect (ground truth) annotations as supervision during representation learning.

Recent advances in time-series data mining have yielded various algorithms and metrics tailored for specific domains, resulting in settings where data remains heavily reliant on extensive domain expertise. To support future machine learning models that generate time-series descriptions, this study introduces **TCube**, a large-scale, domain-neutral dataset containing 1,300 datasets across 13 distinct categories, each with 100 training and testing samples. Curated through a rigorous process involving both automated filtering and manual verification, TCube includes diverse statistical patterns such as trends, cycles, and changes. Accompanying the data is a unified API that exposes standard prediction tasks alongside new correlations between data values and commentaries. Notably, this API provides paired machine-generated comments created by an LLM, offering a unique foundation for training descriptions-focused models.

We examine the Ising model on a Cayley tree of order 2, demonstrating that on this specific structure, the unique Gibbs state exhibits neither translational invariant nor periodic properties under the traditional definition. To address this, the authors propose a generalized concept of translational invariance tailored for Cayley trees, utilizing it to define periodicity in this new framework. Under these conditions, they prove the existence of a unique weakly periodic Gibbs state. Finally, the study establishes the methodology for constructing this state and determine its corresponding potential.

This paper examines a hyperbolic system of causal type defined by $u_{tt} = B(t,x)\partial_x^2 u + C_1(t,x) u_t + C_2 u + F$, subject to the initial-boundary value constraints $[C_3 u + C_4 u_t]_{t=0} = 0$ and $[C_5 u + C_6 u_t]_{t=0} = 0$. The coefficients $C_i$ and the source term $F$ are assumed to be sufficiently smooth and possess bounded $L^\infty$ norms along with temporal and spatial derivatives up to the second order, augmented by a time derivative weighted by a given function. Specifically, these functions must satisfy the condition $|\partial_t^k C_i| + |\partial_t^j \partial_x^l C_i| + |\partial_t^j F| \in L^\infty$ for all $t \geq 0$, $j+k \leq 2$, and $j \leq 1$. Under these assumptions, we establish the well-posedness of the problem for global times.

Term extraction, which involves identifying phrases representing specific technical or generic terms within sentences, is a fundamental aspect of information extraction. The process is significantly more arduous in non-English, specifically agglutinative languages like Japanese, which lack word boundaries and rely on complex linguistic structures, as compared to languages such as English. While many automated systems have been developed, they predominantly favor statistical or rule-based methodologies. This study introduces a new memory-based neural network framework tailored for Japanese term segmentation. Experiments demonstrate that the memory components significantly enhance model performance, surpassing baseline approaches and establishing state-of-the-art results.

As the world's premier programming forum, Stack Overflow (SO) facilitates the exchange of technical knowledge among developers globally. This study examines external links frequently posted on SO, revealing that top-linked sites are predominantly established and long-standing. Furthermore, links to SO itself are distributed across diverse categories, underscoring its multifaceted role in developer education. Link volumes from individual contributing members vary significantly. Despite this diversity, internal SO communication remains the primary channel, surpassing links to external resources in frequency.

Galaxies exhibit vast diversity in their physical attributes, a fact often captured by multi-dimensional taxonomies, yet many numerical simulations currently fail to reproduce this rich variety in galactic properties. Recent studies have explored various methods to achieve simulating galaxy diversity, yet each approach carries its own limitations and assumptions. This review critically evaluates the existing solutions, assessing their respective advantages, disadvantages, and inherent assumptions to determine their viability. Ultimately, we conclude that the most promising future avenue lies in developing or refining the galactic physics themselves.

Clouds & Sensing is dedicated to raising public awareness regarding climate change. Particular attention is given to empowering citizens in various climate knowledge domains, thereby stimulating meaningful discussion and action. Yet, accessing accurate information remains a significant hurdle for the average individual. Clouds & Sensing intends to overcome this barrier by creating a specialized knowledge platform featuring an interactive search interface, curated datasets, and a dedicated app. To ensure the system's reliability, a specialized Cloud of Semantic Web technologies underpins it, leveraging a detailed set of established ontologies. This technical infrastructure enables intelligent, semantic-enhanced searching capabilities. Furthermore, to maintain long-term impact, sustained engagement with diverse user groups is essential; to this end, a specific user study has been designed to gauge interest in and acceptance of the proposed system.

Medical data exhibits inherent symmetry; for instance, the clinical significance of "fever" remains consistent whether framed as a high temperature or "no fever." This observation inspires a novel approach to domain generalization by leveraging such anatomical or logical symmetry to improve learning, where "neglecting" the non-thematic aspect allows the model to focus on the true signal. We formalize this concept as *symmetry-based domain generalization* and introduce *symmetry-based contrastive learning* to enable representations to distinguish intrinsic attributes against symmetric counterparts. Crucially, our method remains applicable even when data symmetry is not预先 known to the learner. We evaluated our framework across two distinct clinical natural language processing tasks: symptom event extraction and high-risk discharge prediction. Results indicate that our model consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both scenarios. Additionally, our approach demonstrates robust efficacy by successfully generalizing to unseen domains, including real-world transfers to a completely new hospital environment. These ablation and benchmark tests confirm both the versatility and potency of our proposed technique.

In the field of robotics, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has proven to be a powerful technique for enabling agents to acquire superior behaviors and policies through continuous interaction and feedback with their environment. However, when it comes to high-stakes domains like autonomous driving, the volatility often produced by RL remains an issue, as standard RL training can result in strategies that are erratic or dangerous. To mitigate this risk and ensure the final policy is safe while delivering top-tier driving results, we introduce a dual-network architecture consisting of separate policy networks, each equipped with its own safety evaluation mechanism. During training, we explicitly filter out policies that fail this safety check, thereby preventing the learning process from discarding promising options or adopting hazardous behaviors. Furthermore, we address the computational expense by suggesting that the safety network can utilize a pre-trained model, significantly lowering the inference and training overhead relative to learning an identical assessment network from scratch. Training the primary policy network employs a state-of-the-art off-line reinforcement learning algorithm tailored for distributional rewards. To validate our approach, we assessed the driving performance of our system against existing methodologies and conducted a thorough examination of the generated trajectories.

In recent years, neural spiking models have gained significant attention for their efficient utilization of computational resources. Nevertheless, ensuring fast convergence and high training efficiency remains a major hurdle. This study introduces a continuous Random Neural Network (RNN) that leverages intrinsic properties of spiking neurons to achieve rapid convergence and effective utilization during training. By eliminating weight initialization requirements and featuring straightforward update mechanisms, this approach fully exploits the space available within spiking neuron states. Furthermore, utilizing gradient-free training fully deploys the inherent efficiency of spiking architectures. An analysis comparing various activation functions reveals that sigmoid-based RNNs offer faster convergence and superior parameter adaptability compared to those employing ReLU. We further introduce an adaptive gradient-free optimizer designed to dynamically refine gradient magnitudes and enhance information propagation throughout the network. Comparative experiments with over a dozen benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive performance and remarkable speed, completing training in under 100 spikes (equivalent to fewer than 100 backward passes). This represents at least an order of magnitude improvement over standard continuous RNNs, making it particularly well-suited for applications on spiking hardware. For comprehensive details, please see: https://www.tandfonline.com/resolve/doi/pdf/10.1080/2472035X.2023.2279303#app-1.

In this study, we calculated spin-polarized strange quark masses within magnetically dominated environments at finite temperature and density, as well as the corresponding Fermi liquid parameters. Our work examines how temperature, the magnetic field strength, Fermi polarization, and spin-polarization specifically influence the mass of a spin-up strange quark. Additionally, we explored the impact of varying the magnetic field, temperature, and spin-polarization on spin-up strange quark stellar stability. The results indicate that while increasing the magnetic field or spin-polarization favors stability, raising the temperature has the opposite effect, thereby reducing stability.

This research introduces Pando, a personal assistant designed within the web browser that leverages user profiles stored in local legacy databases. The study outlines a system architecture, develops specific technologies to overcome regional security constraints, and presents initial evaluations. The paper concludes by exploring Pando's implications for browser-assisted computing and its potential influence on the evolution of personal assistants.

This study presents a robust method for estimating nonlinear eigenvalues within a subset of subsets via adaptive selection. It enables the conversion of a large-scale nonlinear approximation into a smaller-scale linear one. The approach leverages rational interpolation of a carefully defined matrix-valued function, constructed from the problem formulation, ensuring optimal convergence rates are maintained. During the process, an explicit and computable criterion determines whether local approximation accuracy is sufficient. Based on this criterion, the adaptive strategy either subdivides areas that require refinement or aggregates regions where it is not needed. Final results are demonstrated through examples involving the calculation of nonlinear modes associated with drummems.

We demonstrate that every intermediate $\beta$-shift is weakly equivalent to a greedy $\beta$-shift of the form $\beta_{\lambda}^{+s}$ for appropriate values of $\lambda$ and $s$. Specifically, for an existing pair $(\beta,\lambda)$ where $0<\lambda<1$, the corresponding equivalence class containing $\beta_{\lambda}$ consists of all shifts $(\beta'_{\lambda'})^{+\mathbf{s}}$, maintaining the relation $0<\lambda'\leq\lambda<1$.

We introduce a novel method for analyzing confinement and the breaking of chiral symmetry within $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories interacting with fermions in the fundamental representation. These features are encapsulated in the unbroken vacuum by an $N_c$-fold degenerate set of Witten's order parameters, denoted as $\Delta_i^{(f)}$ for $i=1,\dots,N_c$. These parameters correspond to fermion bilinears $\Delta_i^{(f)} = \text{Tr}[\Gamma_i S^{(f)}]$, where $S^{(f)}$ is the fermionic Schwinger-Dyson determinant involving the Dirac matrices $\Gamma_i$ of $SU(N_f)$ global symmetry. Although these order parameters cannot be directly employed to construct confinement- and chiral-symmetry-dependent Euclidean actions, their vacuum expectation values can be accurately approximated via stochastic quantization. Consequently, these stochastic observables serve as highly efficient benchmarks for validating gauge-field configurations that satisfy the Wilsonian confinement criteria. Our numerical evaluations of the $\Delta_i^{(f)}$ demonstrate that configurations generated by the Wilsonian ensemble—specifically those with $SO(N_c)$ gauge groups coupled to $N_f$ flavors of fundamental fermions—satisfie all confinement criteria. This includes the restoration of chiral symmetry at large $N_c$ via the mechanism of dynamical mass generation.

Machine learning models are now integral to high-stakes domains, including healthcare and finance, necessitating a shift toward transparent algorithms that allow users to comprehend and trust system outputs. However, popular ensemble methods, including Random Forests, remain largely opaque due to their intricate construction. This research introduces Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), a novel technique for rendering Random Forest interpretations both global and local by analyzing data features across the forest's component trees. To achieve this, we developed two methods—Disentangled Feature Analysis (DFA) and Disentangled Feature Progression Analysis (DFP)—to isolate how individual features influence predictions even within black-box models. DFA examines feature impact at every node to generate smooth curves, while DFP assesses the significance of feature groups as the model branches diverge. Testing DFA on a text classification dataset and DF P on two tabular benchmarks, alongside a visualization of a Random Forest applied to a text dataset, demonstrated that the approach yields highly accurate representations of machine learning decisions.

Federated Learning (FL) is emerging as a leading framework for privacy-preserving machine learning, enabling mobile devices and data silos to collaboratively train global models without exposing local datasets. Practical FL implementations rely on Secure Enclaves, which offer hardware-based isolation to ensure that sensitive user data remains hidden during processing. However, traditional FL protocols face two significant limitations in this context: first, they discard useful gradient information by discarding it during parameter updates rather than leveraging it; second, they fail to exploit the high performance of modern Secure Enclaves, leaving FL training slower than potentially possible. To address these challenges, we introduce Flatee, a framework that redefines FL operations within Secure Enclaves. Flatee utilizes techniques from Trusted Computation Environment (TCE) coordination to achieve parameter and gradient privacy while simultaneously allowing data analysis by location-aware users. Users with access to specific data locations can verify model component integrity before downloading them, thereby retaining gradient utility and improving computational throughput. Experimental evaluations across diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that Flatee significantly surpasses conventional FL efficiency, delivering faster training speeds and lower communication costs without compromising privacy standards.

As vehicles accumulate more software-controlled features, the extensive regression testing required has become increasingly demanding. A key challenge is that modern high-EU-flipped cars often run on small embedded systems with constrained resources, making it difficult to install the complex, resource-heavy test frameworks commonly used in larger systems. This paper introduces a solution where standard off-the-shelf hardware is paired with a lightweight, flexible Automated Driver Generation (ADG) tool tailored specifically for driver creation in resource-restricted environments. Evaluations on systems with limited footprints demonstrate that the drivers generated by this approach are as effective as those written manually, while significantly cutting down the human effort needed—a factor of seven—thereby supporting larger software updates within a tighter regression schedule.

This paper introduces Timeloops, an end-to-end methodology designed to optimize the system call strategy within containerized microservices. Modern large-scale microservice architectures demand minimal system call latency to maintain peak throughput, necessitating intelligent system call policies. However, existing approaches are ill-equipped for this environment due to challenges posed by containerized architectures. Our contribution is a complete, four-stage pipeline addressing these hurdles. First, a hardware-based trace collection framework efficiently captures comprehensive CPU state information. Second, a specialized memory access model streamlines the modeling of how microservices utilize memory. Third, we employ deep learning techniques to anticipate system call requirements based on integrated models of both data and computational pathways. Fourth, a specialized runtime environment enables rapid, online refinement of these policies to adapt dynamically to varying workloads. Through extensive testing on real microservices, we demonstrate that our learned policies substantially lower system call overhead compared to conventional methods, delivering performance on par with optimal static configurations while offering superior adaptability.

This study investigates linear classification within merch-space forms. We begin by demonstrating that if a set of convexly independent patterns exists in an $N$-dimensional merch-space form, then $N$ must be at least 2 to ensure linear separability, implying limited dimensionality requirements for separability. Next, we examine linear classification within an $N$-dimensional merch-space form under the Lp norm ($P \ge 1$). We introduce an angle $\alpha_P$ between the $(N-P)$ axis and the $(N-P)$ axis, re-expressing separability in terms of this angle. We analyze the properties of $\alpha_P$ across dimensions and establish these using mathematical induction.

The spatial layout of stars within a galactic nucleus, governed by a central supermassive black hole (SMBH), is a critical indicator of galactic evolution. Previous research proposed dividing the stellar density profile into three zones: an inner region dominated by Keplerian orbits, a transitional area, and an outer zone characterized by orbital precession but remaining bound states. However, these studies often relied on arbitrary boundary definitions. This work investigates a more rigorous spatial partition by distinguishing between populations in tight Kepler orbits and those in the exterior domain. We analyze the total light emission from these outer stars, incorporating contributions from both non-relativistic entities and relativistically bound stars. Since the density in tight Kepler orbits is highly sensitive to the presence of compact companions—such as stellar-mass black holes or neutron stars formed from collapsed stars—we explore how an inner SMBH sphere of influence alters the outer luminosity. Specifically, we calculate the ratio of outer-to-outer luminosity to quantify these effects. Our findings indicate that the ratio of outer-to-outer luminosity is a powerful diagnostic tool for detecting the statistical properties of objects within the inner region, provided the SMBH is sufficiently massive and the surrounding cluster is dense enough. For a system like M31, where a massive SMBH exists, this methodology offers a promising new avenue for investigating stellar dynamics and identifying compact objects within their core regions.

The primary goal of this short paper is to examine a simple linear programming simulation example involving four time steps and four distinct scenarios, specifically to compare deterministic Model Predictive Control (MPC) with a random MPC (RMPC). While shorter versions of this exposition appear as simulations in Chapter 7 of my book "Stochastic Modeling, Analysis, and Design of Stochastic Systems" (2020), this treatment provides additional context for MPC and RMPC along with complete mathematical derivations and implementation details using C++.

However, most real-world data are inherently complex, often decomposing naturally into a small set of singular components divided into signal, noise, and outlier groups. This paper introduces a novel agent-based elector model designed to simulate how political parties compete for support. We examine two one-dimensional scenarios to analyze equilibrium states and transition dynamics, focusing on the impact of competing parties with varying tradeoff parameters between species exclusion and coexistence strategies. Our findings confirm a known negative correlation between investment levels in aggressive competition and colonization within such elector parties: an investment pattern that maximizes the capture of new territory also increases the risk of total electoral extinction due to complete exclusion. Conversely, our analysis reveals a relationship between the parameter thresholds determining persistent competition (coexistence) and the efficiency of competition and colonization strategies, showing how tradeoff parameters influence these outcomes under different conditions. We also study how noise levels affect party distribution in electoral spaces where competition and colonization strategies are balanced. Finally, our analysis demonstrates how varying levels of noise interact with competition and colonization tradeoff parameters to affect competition dynamics and coexistence.

This research explores the feasibility of simultaneous photon-magnomechanical (magnon-photon-phononic) entanglement within the cavity magnomechanical framework by integrating coherent quantum feedback. Our analysis reveals that under specific parametric conditions, the proposed feedback-loop architecture enhances the overall entanglement measured by the negativity criterion. Programmable phase plates (PPs), first proposed in 2009, offer a viable method for controlling phase disturbances in light beams. Initially designed for various optical applications—including enhancing resolution in microscopes, increasing image contrast, and stabilizing complex beams for single-molecule imaging in fluorescence—they have not yet addressed high-end phase correction in transmission electron microscopy (TEM). TEM has historically relied on multilap correctors, which use six electrostatic quadrupole coil pairs to compensate for the dominant fifth-order spherical aberrulation ($C_s$) and second-energy-dispersion aberrulation ($C_s^2$). While PPs can replicate the angular phase correction provided by a single quadrupole coil, managing higher-order effects required for sub-angstrom resolution in modern instruments proves more challenging. Specifically, achieving the >99.9% photon transmission typical of modern correctors is difficult with current PP designs, which typically exhibit significantly lower transmission rates. Furthermore, while a single PP configuration cannot fully replicate the combined angular phase corrections from all six quadrupole coil pairs needed for complete $C_s$ and $C_s^2$ compensation, theoretical analysis suggests that specific patterns of phase shifts within an existing 6PP could potentially mimic the net effect of the eight coil systems.

Let $d \ge 1$ be an integer, $\{X_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. random vectors uniformly distributed over the hypercube $\{0,1\}^d$, and $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ denote a multinomial random walk on the $d$-dimensional integer lattice. Specifically, for dimensions $d=2$ we obtain strong asymptotic results as $n \to \infty$ regarding how the walk interacts with both closed and open $L_1$-norm balls.

This quasinormal mode analysis examines the gravitational spectrum of a polymer black hole defined by an improved quantum dynamics that successfully eliminates the classical singularity. By modeling Lorentzian quantum corrections and adapting the Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin framework, we determine both inner and outer horizons where metric components remain finite. An analytical framework based on coordinate transformations is developed to compute effective potentials for Lorentzian gravity. By approximating quantum effects as a Debye model, we calculate specific frequencies to map out this potential. Finally, we validate these findings by comparing them with standard results from general relativity.

Addressing the controversy surrounding the low heat capacity of twisted bilayer graphene at low doping levels, we provide fresh first-principles calculations for the band structures of monolayer graphene and AB-stacked bilayer graphene alongside their specific phonon dispersion relations. These electronic band structures are subsequently utilized within a Monte Carlo framework to derive the finite-temperature density of states (DOS) and carry out heat capacity integrations. Our findings indicate that while twisted bilayer graphene exhibits a more singular van Hove divergence in heat capacity compared to AB-stacked bilayer graphene, the magnitude of this divergence is insufficient to account for the previously reported anomalies. We further calculate the DOS and resulting heat capacity at a finite temperature of 300 K, demonstrating that thermal effects significantly alter both the DOS profile and the heat capacity. Notably, we observe that the heat capacity of twisted bilayer graphene at low to moderate doping levels is approximately 10% lower than that of monolayer graphene.

Speech synthesis systems are typically developed through two separate stages: first, creating a mask to identify the most influential speech contexts from the speaker's personal history, and second, learning a function for the speech generation decoder using only these selected features. In this study, we introduce a unified framework for speech synthesis that integrates these traditionally disjointed phases. By training the decoder on random mask subsets during synthesis, we demonstrate that this approach improves generation quality and enhances the model's ability to generalize. Furthermore, the proposed system requires pre-specified mask dimensions and adapts the mask size specifically to each individual speaker. Empirical evaluations on the Test Set A of the 2020 Turing Award Challenge confirm that our method achieves state-of-the-art results.

Estimating the conditional mean is fundamental to many statistical and machine learning tasks. In this study, we introduce an algorithm named Laplace PPP which operates by first projecting both input and output spaces into a shared space using a randomized projection. Once this step is complete, mean regression is performed in the projected space employing a projection-based method. Finally, the conditionally averaged estimates are derived through averaging the projections of the original data. We provide theoretical justification for this approach, including convergence rates for the prediction errors. Comparative analyses demonstrate that Laplace PPP achieves significantly lower prediction errors than standard PPP variants while maintaining the same asymptotic efficiency. Numerical simulations across synthetic and real-world datasets further support these claims, highlighting the model's robustness.

While classifiers have been successfully deployed in security-critical areas like spam filtering and facial recognition, they remain vulnerable to adversarial examples: minimally modified, human-undetectable inputs labeled incorrectly by the model. Although prior research has largely addressed these threats within static image classification, classifier performance remains fragile in dynamic environments where attackers possess equal or greater flexibility in image generation than defenders. In this work, we introduce a new assault vector we term "Generative Adversarial Attacks" (GAA). Unlike traditional attack methods, GAAs do not begin with an authenticated, benign input but instead synthesize entirely fake images to deceive classifiers. This paper defines the core problem of GAA, proposes two novel algorithms for executing such attacks, and offers comprehensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that current anti-adversarial defense strategies are ineffective at countering GAA. Finally, we analyze classifier behavior during GAA to identify classifier properties that resist these specific synthetic assaults.

This study examines climate change conspiracy theories within Facebook discussions, with the aim of identifying theoretical underpinnings that sustain misinformation networks. The analysis focuses on posts from October 2019 to October 2020, drawn from eighteen specialized climate-related page accounts, many of which have since been deactivated due to policy violations regarding deceptive content.

Data processing involved extracting posts, associated pages, mutual connections on the social network, individual post interactions, author networks, and comment threads. These records were subsequently tagged using established networks from Social Media Commons and mapped onto Hoard's (1976) social movement frameworks to enrich existing datasets. The networks were finally assessed through network analysis techniques to investigate their structural properties.

Findings indicate that existing theoretical models require significant adaptation for effective deployment in social media contexts. Although these models offer valuable context for understanding climate skepticism online, they fall short in fully explaining how digital networks restructure traditional information ecosystems. Specifically, evidence suggests that Social Media Commons theory can still illuminate underlying forces driving climate denial, but only when strategically modified to account for the distinct characteristics of digital interaction.

This study examines searches for dark matter generated alongside isolated top quarks or top-quark pairs during proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The analysis utilizes a data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 13.6 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Events featuring jets, isolated leptons (electrons or muons), and missing transverse momentum are examined. These selections target three theoretical production channels: single $t\bar{t}$ associated production, or simplified models involving vector boson fusion or associated production of a dark matter particle with a single top quark. Findings are contrasted with predictions for the Standard Model and various simplified dark matter theories, yielding constraints on the production cross sections within these frameworks.

We demonstrate that for an $n$-extranged derivation category $\mathbf{D}(\mathcal{A})$ associated with an $n$-expositively resolved algebra $\mathcal{A}$, there exists $\mathbf{n}$-extrange Serre duality. When fields of study are selected in sequential order over a person's life, the aggregate number of years spent in various majors serves as an endogenous treatment variable subject to unobserved confounders. To address this, we develop an instrumental variables framework designed for choosing treatments at multiple stages without specifying the exact timing of causal effects. We then apply this methodology to analyze how different fields impact individual wages, utilizing high school major choices and the relative popularity of fields as instruments. Our results indicate that, on average, men gain approximately 13% and women approximately 9% more wages by choosing STEM over non-STEM majors, while also estimating the returns specifically to each individual field of study.

We explore a four-dimensional $\lambda\phi^4$ scalar field within a simple cubic lattice framework in the context of cosmology, specifically focusing on early universe scenarios. Through a Monte Carlo simulation, the dynamics of this system are investigated, demonstrating a clear link between the model's parameter space and its observed flatness. We analyze how varying $\lambda$ influences the system's behavior, noting that specific values lead to effective scalar domination characteristic of Brans-Dicke type models. In selected cases, particularly regarding flatness, this flatness emerges naturally rather than being imposed, and we identify that certain flatness optima correspond to a phase transition. Furthermore, certain model configurations yield effective inflation capable of suppressing curvature, a result we discuss regarding its implications for real-world applications.

Image segmentation is a critical task in computer vision, widely applied across various fields such as pattern recognition, face identification, medical analysis, and machine vision. While numerous models addressing image segmentation have emerged over the years, this study introduces a fresh framework by integrating completion mechanisms into existing segmentation models. This approach aims to enhance overall performance. Although some models based on completion principles are available, they are rarely applied within segmentation contexts. We introduce two specific techniques, averaging-based completion and gradient-guided completion, designed to leverage complementary information between segments and accelerate convergence. Furthermore, by reformulating completion processes as variational problems and deriving them into difference equation formats suitable for GPU implementation, both methods can be efficiently executed. Experimental validation across diverse image sets confirms that models incorporating these techniques outperform state-of-the-art methods in speed and segmentation accuracy.

Heavy black holes, whether spinning or charged, can theoretically amplify ultralight bosons through the superradiant effect. As these bosons accumulate, they form a cloud around the black hole; once this cloud reaches the point of quenching, the resulting system functions as an oscillator where its quinquinary quanta determine the oscillation's frequency. By comparing the quinquunity of this cloud with the quinquunity of photons emitted by oscillating black holes, we can analyze their relationship. Since direct measurement of boson cloud quinquunity remains impossible, researchers instead examine spin quinquanty in two distinct regimes: non-relativistic and highly relativistic states. In this study, by measuring spin quinquanty via gravitational radiation, we can derive constraints on the mass range of bosons. Specifically, by utilizing spin quinquanty in the highly relativistic state for supermassive black holes, we can narrow down the exclusion regions for new boson masses by a factor of 100 compared to previous methods employing monochromatic radiation frequency.

Achieving high-fidelity simulations for neuromorphic networks is critical for interpreting their capabilities and guiding future design iterations. On the Loihi neuromorphic processor, such limited-hardware access is restricted, necessitating the use of software-based emulators that mirror chip behavior to facilitate in-depth analysis. This environment leverages the Clyde scalar spiking neural network emulator, offering an independent verification layer against other Loihi software and hardware systems.

Although numerous optical trapping methods exist for manipulating individual atoms and molecules, none currently enable the precise trapping and control required for high-resolution imaging or sensing. This limitation stems from the large physical footprint of these systems, which hinders their use in achieving the necessary accuracy. We introduce a compact optical trapping scheme driven by a planar integrated microphotonics platform that successfully captures individual molecules at an interface while maintaining single-molecule fluorescence signal strength. Our approach breaks previous limitations by demonstrating molecular trapping within a compact optical configuration, paving the way for further advancements in sensitivity through trapping control at chip-scale dimensions.

This study presents an analytical framework for describing how a black hole accretes matter from a sphere with a finite initial radius, explicitly accounting for rotation. While previous research on spherical collapse typically assumed either an infinitely large source or a uniform velocity distribution, this work models the initial state more realistically as a finite sphere where specific angular momentum $L$ follows a power-law profile, $L \propto r^q$, based on these assumptions, this model demonstrates how a black hole can engulf the entire sphere, even when angular momentum barriers are significant. As the accretion process begins, the black hole's mass grows, causing its event horizon to expand. Once the radius of this horizon surpasses the angular momentum's characteristic scale, $r_{\rm Ang}(M_{\rm BH})\sim L^{1/(1-q)}$, angular momentum is effectively incorporated, initiating the collapse of all infalling matter. Consequently, the black hole's mass doubles approximately every time it increases its radius by a factor of two, following $M_{\rm BH}(t)\sim t^{2/(1-q)}$. This mechanism suggests that the characteristic accretion rate is primarily determined by how angular momentum scales with radius in systems like galaxy mergers. Furthermore, the model predicts the emergence of a quasar phase immediately after the black hole's mass surpasses a critical threshold, $M_{\rm crit}\sim 10^9 M_{\odot}$.

This study examines how an atom interacts with a highly reflective flat mirror in classical backgrounds, focusing on scenarios where the atom moves parallel or perpendicular to the mirror surface. We formulate general equations for the induced transition rates across all atomic energy levels, accounting for both excitation and de-excitation processes triggered by uniform translation or atomic braking. Our results demonstrate that time-varyial atomic velocity generates induced transitions even for atoms initially in their ground state. Furthermore, we derive exact formulas for emitting atoms and calculate precisely which frequencies correspond to single or double photon transitions (radiation with a double energy gap). Finally, we link these radiation characteristics to classical atomic dipole moments, drawing parallels to phenomena observed in moving or oscillating classical dipoles.

The massive star formation region Wester 2 (Wester 2) is one of the most notable clusters in the Milky Way, renowned for its extreme mass stars. This study presents the outcomes of a high-resolution (0.3") photometric and spectroscopic analysis of W3-33 (W33), one of three candidate embedded proto-cluster proto-star clusters within W2, with the aim of distinguishing potential W2 cluster members from local background sources and the W2 cluster itself. Our observations reveal that W33 is characterized by an abundance of background sources and foreground stars, rendering it unsuitable for studies focused exclusively on massive star formation within this region. However, W33 is positioned adjacent to another cluster candidate, the W2-1 cloud, which contains a higher concentration of Herbig massive stars. These data suggest that W33 and the W2-1 cloud may be fragmented substructures of a larger cluster complex. Furthermore, spectral classification of the stars in W333 shows a significant proportion of H-striated objects, indicating that mass transfer from accreted material to the central star has not yet ceased.

This study addresses the problem of locating normalized ground states for this Choud "bipahign" (biharmonic) equation involving Ritz integral (Choqueter integral), where the potential function $V(x)$ is allowed to experience essential growth. The nonlinearity function $f(x,|u|^2)$ is designed such that the whole function belongs to the exponential scale. To deal with the constrained minimization challenge, we employ a quantitative analysis based upon the "double mountain pass" concept. The approach utilizes the "double mountain pass" concept, which turns out to be useful in addressing this specific type of problem with these specific constraints and conditions.

Handwritten document recognition systems are significantly hampered by poor print quality, which causes noise in high-resolution historical images and leads to blur and missing data in low-resolution scans. While many enhancement methods focus solely on visual aesthetics, often neglecting visual semantics and failing to deliver satisfactory results for complex ancient scripts. This study introduces MADNet, a multi-task adversective network designed to jointly optimize image resolution and written semantics through an end-to-end process, rather than relying on separate isolated steps. The architecture incorporates a residual generator for upscaling, two discriminators to distinguish real from synthetic images across both overall structure and textual details, and an anomaly detector aimed at identifying non-text regions to guide the synthesis toward accuracy. Trained using paired historical documents alongside their corresponding semantic segmentation masks, the model leverages these semantic cues to produce high-resolution outputs superior to state-of-the-art methods, as verified by improved metric scores. Furthermore, the enhanced images facilitate better performance in downstream recognition systems. Experimental outcomes demonstrate not only enhanced image quality but also increased accuracy in handwritten document image analysis.

Recent ID card applications have increasingly adopted Optical Character Recognition (OCR) due to its cost-effectiveness and convenience, a trend reflected in the 2019 launch of OCR4ID by the Indonesian government. This study introduces a OCR-based Indonesian identity card extraction system developed in early pandemic conditions, responding to restrictions on Indonesian citizens traveling abroad. While OCR4ID is functional, it exhibits inaccuracies; consequently, this research enhances its performance by integrating Natural Language Processing techniques. Specifically, the application leverages WordNet and an Indonesian synonym database to refine name matching and correction. Experiments were conducted on 300 images, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.91 and an accuracy of 91%.

In vehicular communication, link quality estimation is essential for enabling applications, although IEEE 802.11p defines specific standards only—lacking explicit quality estimation protocols—which this study seeks to address using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), a prominent deep-learning technique capable of capturing temporal dependencies. By employing this layer, we can mitigate unnecessary feedback, reduce system overhead, and enhance estimation accuracy. Results indicate that this approach significantly outperforms existing techniques regarding both precision and application-specific performance.

Data curation for astronomical image analysis involves time-consuming manual labeling to create supervised datasets. However, we introduce a generative approach that avoids the need for labeled data entirely. Designed to map grayscale images to their color equivalents, this technique fills voids by synthesizing tags for unlabeled samples, thereby expanding existing labeled datasets efficiently. We evaluated the system using 1,000 randomly selected HIgh-z Automatable Classification Explanations (3DHAE) images drawn from the Image Catalog for Deep Learning and Classification (IMC DLC). The resulting labeled dataset was then employed to train Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) on various image transformations. Finally, the system applied these learned mappings to generate tags for unlabeled images, demonstrating that creating labels through astronomical image colorization via GANs is both more rapid and more cost-effective than traditional human curation.

The paper presents a new approach to neural network architecture design, inspired by the Universal Approximation Theorem which any network must satisfy. This study proposes constructing networks as direct implementations of this theorem, resulting in a simpler, more efficient structure that eliminates the need for explicit weight parameters. We detail the network's components, advantages, and theoretical underpinnings, demonstrating through numerical experiments on regression and classification tasks that this simplified architecture offers training efficiency and performance on par with traditional models.

In 2021, the ECFA established its Researcher's Committee for Early Career (ECER), a group formed to unite ECFA members at the PhD graduate stage or below four years post-PhD. That same year, we organized our inaugural workshop and one virtual meeting. Work continued in 2022 with two virtual meetings and the organization of the Second Researcher's Early Career Conference (CEDEC 2022) held online amidst globally widespread lockdowns. The upcoming year of office will focus on expanding ECER activities and strengthening the committee's presence and research within ECFA.

Recent advancements in the development of dual metasurfaces have demonstrated their efficacy in correcting the phase gradients of line ripple propagation at the interface, thereby achieving superior optical performance. However, a definitive quantitative metric for optical quality line ripples has been missing. Addressing this gap, this study introduces a formal formulation based on the angular spectral approach to characterize line ripples at meta-interfaces. We apply this framework to evaluate angular spectra in systems comprising conventional, single-layer, and dual metasurfaces, allowing for a rigorous comparison of optical quality. Furthermore, by utilizing numerically supported simulations, the line ripple propagation properties were examined across various configurations—including homogeneous media, actual and theoretical scenarios involving air glass and metal—along with simulations involving both dielectric and conductive materials. Finally, numerical support was used to demonstrate a practical application: utilizing dual metasurfaces to transform line ripples into Bessel beams, which were subsequently converted into Gaussian beams via a complementary phase-gradient metasurface.

Cognitive science and the merging of computational power with machine and robotic capabilities have created opportunities to build scalable, multi-agent learning systems involving humans and robots. These networks must operate across diverse hardware types and heterogeneous agent capabilities. To enable effective teaching and learning between humans and robots at this scale, each participant requires a flexible, scalable architecture that supports complex cognitive processes. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop the theoretical basis for cognitive AI, apply it to the design of architecture, and validate these approaches through a prototype testbed.

A sample estimation of the population level typically utilizes the mean; however, when sampling bias exists, the mean may be inadequate, making the median the preferred alternative. Correspondingly, the distributed parameter most closely matched by the sample's mean absolute deviation (AD) is its population mean, yet this same value is sampling biased. In contrast, population mean AD cannot be unbiasedly estimated using the sample's mean. Conversely, when calculated around the sample median, both the population mean (at the median) and the variation in AD around it become sampling biased quantities.

The current study demonstrates that these estimators remain biased despite applying transformations to the observations themselves. Specifically, we derive the asymptotic bias of the mean AD around the sample median at an accelerated sampling pace of $O\left(n^{-1}\right)$ via the delta method. Using this insight, we implement a correction based on the bootstrapping process. This allows us to construct unbiased sample estimators for the population mean mean AD around the sample's median at an asymptotic speed of $O\left(n^{-1}\right)$ without requiring the normal distribution assumption.

Our findings indicate that this bias-corrected estimator of mean AD around the sample median performs better than the classical two-pass estimator in estimating population mean mean AD around the mean.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying semantic connections between subject-object pairs within sentences. Although Exponential Amounts (EA) of relational data already exist within projects like Wikidata and Facebook's Open Graph, widely-used Auto-Encoders for sentences fail to fully benefit from these resources due to format incompatibility. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that merges knowledge graph (KG) representations with sentence analysis to maximize the utilization of existing relational data. By using potential relationships predicted by our model to filter sentence-derived relation candidates, the system enhances RE performance. Empirical evaluation on three datasets confirms that this approach significantly boosts results, particularly for tasks where pre-training data is scarce. The code for this project is available on GitHub.

Analyzing quarkonium dissociation in a anisotropic QCD medium within $d+1$ dimensions at finite chemical potential is addressed using an open color source approach. The finite temperature Quasi-particle approach in N-dimensional space has been utilized to establish the Debye mass and solve Schrödinger's equation for various quarkonium states using the Hartree-Fock model. The results show that the binding energy, radial excitation, real and imaginary components of the mass, as well as the dissociation temperature, are significantly impacted by both spatial anisotropy and the chemical potential. Additionally, we have established that quarkonium binding energy decreases with increasing anisotropy and chemical potential values, while the dissociation temperature rises. Conversely, the medium's opacity exhibits the opposite trend. These quarkonium properties show a strong dependence on the chosen spatial dimension.

Tb$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$ exhibits complex magnetic and electronic behaviors stemming from the interplay between the magnetic rare-earth ions and one-electron correlations and strong spin-orbit coupling associated with Ru$^{4+}$. In this study, we investigate the magnetic and transport characteristics of Tb$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$ under an applied dc magnetic field, focusing on its response to field orientation and strength. Our findings reveal intricate zero-field thermal dependence of specific heat and resistivity, alongside a newly discovered magnetic field orientation-dependent transition. Specifically, at temperatures below 2.5 K, dc susceptibility measurements indicate that rare-earth ions form a 3D antiferromagnetic structure, while Ru chains—characterized by alternating bond lengths and acting as spin 3/2 systems with significant single-ion anisotropy—are influenced significantly by the rare-earth moments. Unlike previous reports, our data show that this low-temperature transition is sensitive to both field orientation and strength. A significant hurdle in functional regression is identifying smooth periodic representations. While splines are commonly employed for smooth approximation, their fixed basis often results in poor generalization outside the training set. To address this, we introduce Modulated Periodic Splines (ModPS), a new functional framework. This approach combines standard splines with complex exponential modulations. ModPS offers three primary advantages: first, it achieves smooth generalization across the entire domain; second, it provides an explicit form for the posterior under a simple Bayesian setup; and third, it demonstrates empirically as an effective tool for periodic feature discovery in regression tasks.

Many statistical and machine learning issues involve distinct target distributions conditioned on covariate shifts. While GANs and VAEs have proven effective for learning the target distribution while marginalizing out confounders, they require samples from the causal inputs, which may not be accessible in practice. This paper introduces a new semi-generative framework that incorporates causal and effect structures while allowing for the incorporation of additional, unmeasured confounders that influence both the inputs and outputs. Our proposed method, GASAC (Generative Approach for Shift Adjustment in Causal contexts), enables the estimation of the conditional distribution given only causal effects and covariate data. We demonstrate the validity of our approach using both synthetic datasets and a high-profile causal dataset in our experimental evaluation, while also conducting an ablation study to assess the impact of causal graph misspecification on its robustness.

Deep learning represents a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, driving breakthroughs in high-profile areas such as computer vision, natural language processing, and machine translation. Despite these advances, the underlying operational mechanisms of these systems remain poorly understood, often described in existing literature as opaque "black boxes." Consequently, researchers have drawn parallels between deep learning's training process and biological neuron evolution through natural selection, seeking to unravel its intricate structures.

This literature review explores that unknown terrain by focusing specifically on the geometric aspects of deep learning. It examines two critical phenomena: the emergence of low-dimensional manifolds within input data and the high dimensionality inherent in layer outputs. By grounding the discussion in differential geometry, we aim to elucidate these mechanisms, thereby contributing to a clearer comprehension of deep learning's inner workings and furthering its integration with mathematics.

We demonstrate that the phenomenon of main effect dominance in screening designs is tied to the minimization of the cubic distance function, whereas robustness, conversely, relies on minimizing the distance function with an exponent of two. Additionally, we address three distinct categories of arrays: those that are both symmetric and dominant in main effects, those that are symmetric and robust, and those that are non-sequential yet symmetricless, all sharing balanced properties. We further present algorithms for constructing such designs based on modular arithmetic and polynomials over finite fields. Our work concludes by highlighting future research opportunities within this field.

As the reliance on machine learning (Jet tagging) increases within particle physics research, the growing sophistication of these algorithms has made developing accurate models difficult to unravel. Within this paper, we employ Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP) alongside expert variables to interpret the Jet tagging models at an input level. The methodology utilizes LRP along with deep learning (JET tagging) to interpret the Jet tagging processes. Additionally, the paper provides a dual generalization of Abel's identity and discusses a foundation in complex analysis for these results.

We examine the relationship between momentum operators and Killing vector fields, specifically focusing on those where the constituent vector fields are tangent to geodesic integral curves. In this study, a specific class of such Killing vectors is presented, enabling an explicit description of the associated momentum operators. Furthermore, by leveraging operators defined through a specific set of Killing vectors, a decomposition method for general elements within the operator domain is developed. Additionally, several applications of this decomposition approach are explored. Although preliminary, these findings suggest promising directions for future investigation.

An increasingly prevalent challenge in Monte Carlo simulations of fermionic systems is the sign problem, a difficulty that grows exponentially with system size and can effectively paralyze larger systems. Recently, neural network-based approaches have emerged as a promising solution. However, these methods typically rely on real-valued networks that suffer from exponentially declining signal-to-noise ratios due to inherent precision limitations. This study introduces the use of complex-valued neural networks instead, demonstrating that they significantly alleviate both the Hubbard sign problem and associated signal-to-signal deterioration. These findings offer a substantial advance for future MC applications in diverse fermionic domains.

We examine a large class of composite models featuring the Higgs as a composite state, focusing on scenarios where the Higgs acquires mass through the mixing of multiple composite degrees of freedom. We term these frameworks Composite Mixed Higgs (CMH) theories. In our analysis, we identify the general structural characteristics of these models and demonstrate that they consistently involve hidden scalar sectors which exhibit strong interactions even at low energy scales. We propose specific realizations of CMH using gauge interactions, providing further analytical evidence for the prevalence and functional necessity of these strongly bound Higgs components. Ultimately, we argue from first principles that both hidden and strongly bound scalar elements are intrinsic features of composite Higgs sectors, a conclusion supported by our findings.

This proposed work is to be the first to empirically validate these connections using perceptual theories alongside a comprehensive analysis of perceptual phenomena. Understanding these perceptions is crucial, but it is also a key component in VR. By quantifying their impact, researchers can begin addressing them, potentially turning this challenge into an advantage.

This study investigates the binary system creation resulting from the fragmentation of a rotating collapsing core into a two-body configuration. Utilizing idealized models with varying total masses but consistent e-folding radii and uniform initial rotation parameters, we conducted high-resolution simulations. We examined key outcomes, including the final masses of the two bodies, their separation distances, the number density at their common boundary within the separation zone, and the ratio of their angular momentum to orbital momentum. We further analyzed how these variables depend on the system's total mass and explored the physical mechanisms driving these dependencies. Additionally, we compared the properties of bodies within equal-mass pairs to those in unequal-mass pairs. We suggest that increasing the mass ratio between fragments requires lower initial mass concentration and/or a higher degree of angular momentum within the system. These conditions facilitate fragmentation into distant, widely separated unequal-mass binaries characterized by a lower separation density and a reduced angular momentum-to-orbital-momentum ratio. Finally, we contrast these findings with standard equal-mass binary systems and those featuring masses separated by orders of magnitude.

We introduce a new method called MArcowitz-Kalman filter-based autonomous analysis of features, or M-ar-K-FAC, which merges the autonomous analysis of features (MArcowitz) with the Kalman filter. While AKF can learn the parameters of the Analysis of Features algorithm using the Kalman filter approach, it requires the user to specify the initial measurement noise covariance ($R$) in the Kalman filter, an issue that MAArK-FAC resolves. The proposed algorithm is capable of simultaneously estimating the parameters of the Analysis of Features and the measurement noise covariance ($R$) without prior user input. Several simulations demonstrate the superior performance of this method in handling nonstationary scenarios compared to both the AKF and standard K-FAC algorithms.

This study investigates whether choiceless polynomial time (CPT) can be contained within extended polynomial calculus (EPC) when these logics are applied to distinguish non-isomorphic structures in the class of bounded-treewidth graphs. Although prior work has independently analyzed this question within bounded-arithmetic graphs and bounded-peano formulas—achieving a separation in both frameworks, with CPT being strictly weaker than EPC on these classes—we provide a distinct proof utilizing graph isomorphism. In this context, we demonstrate that CPT is strictly weaker than EPT by applying their respective capabilities to differentiate two specific, non-isomorphic graphs.
